answer.rationale: The contract expires in 14 days so I cannot defer (c5) without risking service lapse on a line running at 94% with no buffer. Switching primary (c2) or adding a second source (c3) both require ramp time that does not exist before expiry and would inflate delivery risk on the constrained component. Renewal-as-is (c1) preserves stability but ignores finance's 18% mandate and leaves recoverable margin on the table. Memory c4 is the highest-leverage signal: a renewal-cycle renegotiation with the incumbent moved both price and terms, and c1 confirms two cycles of stable integration with no migration pain. The same conditions hold today — incumbent is in place, line is hot, and contract is at expiry — so negotiating renewal with the incumbent is the path that captures the c4-style savings while preserving c1's stability. I am verifying c4 (to confirm the price-and-terms lever still applies) and c1 (to confirm no integration risk has emerged since day 21) before committing. One source of residual uncertainty: whether finance's 18% target is achievable purely through renegotiation or whether a partial second-source action will be needed in the next review; I am preserving that question rather than collapsing it.
